levels.name: Reactive
levels.short: Not in place, or only when something goes wrong.

levels.name: Started
levels.short: First steps taken, not yet a routine.

levels.name: Measured
levels.short: Followed and measured; gaps are closed.

levels.name: Sustained
levels.short: Sustained and improving by the team itself.

dimensions.name: 5S and visual management
statements: Only what is needed for the work is in the area; unneeded items are red-tagged and removed.
Every tool, material, scanner and trolley has a marked place, and a missing item is visible at a glance.
Cleaning and checking run on a schedule with an owner, and the schedule is kept.
Floor markings, labels and boards show normal and abnormal without having to ask anyone.
A 5S audit is held on a schedule, its score is posted, and its findings are closed.
levels: Items with no owner pile up in corners and aisles; people search for tools, scanners and pallet jacks every shift.
A first red-tag sort has been done and some places are marked, but markings are partial or worn and clutter returns within weeks.
Every item has a marked, labelled place; a cleaning plan with owners hangs in the area and is mostly kept.
5S audits run on a schedule, the score is posted with its trend, and each finding gets an owner and a date.
The area's own people run the audits and raise the standard after each round; a visitor finds anything in 30 seconds.
dimensions.advice: Start in one zone, not the whole area: red-tag what is not needed, mark a place for what stays, and score a first 5S audit as the baseline. Repeat the audit every week until the score holds.
dimensions.action: Red-tag sort and first 5S audit in {area}
dimensions.check: 5S audit score at the start and four weeks later

dimensions.name: Standard work
statements: The main tasks (receiving, picking, cleaning a room, loading a route) have a written standard with steps, key points and the reason for each key point.
The standards hang where the work is done, are current, and show who changed them last and when.
People work to the standard: an observation of the task matches what is written.
When someone finds a better way, the standard is changed and every shift is trained on the change.
levels: Everyone does the task their own way; the method depends on who trained them; results differ by person and shift.
Standards exist for some tasks, but they sit in a binder or the system, are out of date, or describe the ideal rather than the real work.
Standards for the main tasks are posted at the workplace, current, and used to train new starters; most people follow them.
Leaders observe adherence on a schedule; each deviation is either corrected or used to improve the standard.
The standard is the baseline for improvement: the people who do the work change it several times a year, with time and quality measured before and after.
dimensions.advice: Take the one task with the most variation between people and write its standard with the team: steps, key points and the reason for each. Post it at the workplace and observe it once on each shift.
dimensions.action: Write and post the standard for the task with the most variation in {area}
dimensions.check: Observation on each shift: the work matches the standard

dimensions.name: Daily management and KPIs
statements: The area holds a short daily meeting at a board at a fixed time, and it starts and ends on time.
Yesterday's results for safety, quality, delivery and cost are on the board against a target before the meeting starts.
A missed target leads to an action with an owner and a date, and open actions are reviewed at the next meeting.
A problem the team cannot solve goes to the next level the same day, and the answer comes back.
levels: No regular meeting; numbers come in a weekly e-mail or not at all; the team hears about problems from complaints.
A meeting happens on most days, but without a board or with numbers that are days old; it is mostly announcements.
A daily stand-up at the board with yesterday's KPIs against targets; a red KPI gets an action, though follow-up is uneven.
Board, KPIs and action list are kept every day; actions close on time; escalation to the next level runs on a fixed schedule.
Shift, area and site meetings follow each other within the morning; the board drives the day's decisions and the KPIs show a lasting improvement.
dimensions.advice: Hold a 10-minute stand-up at a board at the same time every day: yesterday's safety, quality, delivery and cost against target, and one action with an owner for each red number. Review the open actions first.
dimensions.action: Start a daily 10-minute board meeting with KPIs against target in {area}
dimensions.check: Meetings held on time and actions closed by their date, for four weeks

dimensions.name: Problem solving
statements: A problem is first described with facts: what, where, when and how many, compared with the standard.
A recurring problem is worked to its root cause (5 Whys, fishbone or A3) before a countermeasure is chosen.
Customer complaints and serious defects get a structured response (8D or similar) with containment, root cause and a check that it worked.
The effect of every countermeasure is checked with data a few weeks later, and the lesson is shared with other shifts or areas.
levels: Firefighting: the same problems return every week; blame or a quick fix ends the discussion; nothing is written down.
Some problems are analysed, usually after an escalation; 5 Whys is known but stops at the first answer or at a person.
Recurring problems get a 5 Whys or an A3 with a root cause and a countermeasure; most are closed, though the effect is not always checked.
Problem solving is tracked: opened and closed, time to close, recurrence; each countermeasure is verified with data.
Front-line staff solve most problems themselves with one simple method; serious cases run as 8D or A3 and the lessons reach other areas.
dimensions.advice: Pick the problem that came back most often last month and take it through 5 Whys with the people who see it, down to a cause you can act on. A customer complaint or a serious defect gets an 8D; a bigger problem an A3.
dimensions.action: Take the most frequent recurring problem in {area} to its root cause
dimensions.check: The problem has not returned four weeks after the countermeasure

dimensions.name: Flow and pull
statements: The value stream of the area is mapped with its lead time, queues and waits, and the map is less than a year old.
Work moves in small, regular batches rather than in big waves (orders, rooms, routes, pallets).
Replenishment is pulled by real use (kanban cards, bins, min/max) rather than pushed by a forecast or a habit.
Work in process and queues are limited and visible, so a jam is noticed before it reaches the customer.
levels: Work arrives in waves and piles up between steps; staff are idle, then overloaded; stock and queues are noticed when they run out or overflow.
The bottleneck is known and some buffers are sized, but work is still planned in big batches and chasing urgent orders is normal.
A current-state map exists; the main flow has a fixed sequence and limits; kanban or min/max runs for the main materials.
Lead time and work in process are measured every week; the work is levelled over the day; kanban quantities are sized from demand data.
A future-state map is being put in place step by step; the flow is smooth over the week; queues and lead time keep falling.
dimensions.advice: Map the value stream of the area on one sheet with its lead time and where the work waits. Then level the work over the day and size the kanban for the main materials from real demand.
dimensions.action: Map the current value stream of {area} with lead time and queues
dimensions.check: Lead time measured on the map, and again after the first change

dimensions.name: Quality at the source
statements: Each step checks its own work before passing it on, so errors are found where they are made.
Common errors are prevented by design: scanners, colour codes, checklists, fixtures or system blocks (poka-yoke).
First-time-right (or the defect rate) is measured per step and shown to the team.
Anyone can stop the work or call for help when something is wrong, and is thanked for doing it.
levels: Errors are found by the customer or the next shift; a check at the end is the only one; mistakes are blamed on people.
Checks exist at a few steps, mostly done by supervisors; defects are counted, but not by step or cause.
Self-checks are part of the standard at the main steps; the main error types have a poka-yoke or a checklist; first-time-right is measured.
Defects are tracked by step and cause; the top risks are in an FMEA; each poka-yoke is tested on a schedule to see that it still works.
New processes are designed with error-proofing from the start; stopping for a defect is normal and quick; first-time-right holds at target.
dimensions.advice: Take the error type that reaches the customer most often and find the step where it is made. Put a poka-yoke or a self-check there, and rank the remaining risks of the process in an FMEA.
dimensions.action: Error-proof the step where the most frequent defect in {area} is made
dimensions.check: First-time-right of that step before and four weeks after

dimensions.name: Maintenance (TPM)
statements: Operators check their equipment every day (forklifts, conveyors, scanners, carts, vehicles) on a short checklist.
Preventive maintenance is planned by date or by use, and the plan is kept.
Breakdowns and their downtime are recorded, and a repeated breakdown is analysed for its cause.
Equipment performance (availability, OEE or downtime per week) is measured and visible to the team.
levels: Equipment runs until it breaks; nobody owns the daily check; parts and repairs are sought after the failure has happened.
A service plan exists for the big equipment, but intervals slip; faults are reported by word of mouth; breakdown records are incomplete.
Daily operator checks with a checklist on the main equipment; preventive maintenance mostly on time; breakdowns logged with their downtime.
MTBF, MTTR or OEE are tracked; repeated failures get a root cause analysis; the plan is adjusted to the failure history.
Operators and technicians improve the equipment together; unplanned downtime is rare and falling; new equipment is chosen for easy maintenance.
dimensions.advice: Put every piece of equipment the area depends on into a maintenance plan with its interval, and give operators a two-minute daily check. Record each breakdown with its downtime so OEE or MTBF can be measured.
dimensions.action: Put the equipment of {area} in a maintenance plan with daily operator checks
dimensions.check: Plan kept on time and breakdowns logged with downtime for one month

dimensions.name: Leadership routines
statements: Leaders at each level have a written leader standard work: what they check each day and each week, and when.
Leaders go to the floor (gemba) on a schedule to see the work, ask and coach, not only when there is a problem.
Leaders check that standards are followed and that the actions from the board are closed.
Leaders coach people to solve problems themselves rather than giving them the answer.
levels: Leaders are in the office or on the phone; they come to the floor when something goes wrong; their day is run by e-mails and escalations.
Some leaders walk the floor, but without a fixed time or purpose; what they check depends on the person.
Leader standard work is written for the main roles, with daily and weekly checks; gemba walks happen most weeks, with notes.
The next level reviews adherence to leader standard work; gemba findings become actions with owners; the routines hold in busy weeks.
The routines are how the site is run; leaders coach with questions; the routines are improved like any other standard.
dimensions.advice: Write the leader standard work for the area's leader: what to check each day and week, and when. Add one gemba walk a week with a purpose, and let the next level check that both happen.
dimensions.action: Write leader standard work and a weekly gemba walk for {area}
dimensions.check: Routine kept in four of four weeks, checked by the next level

dimensions.name: People and skills
statements: A skills matrix shows who can do which task and at what level, and it is current.
Every key task has at least two or three trained people per shift, so one absence does not stop the work.
New starters and people changing task are trained on the standard (for example with TWI job instruction) and signed off.
People take part in improvements, and their ideas are recognised.
levels: Training is by shadowing whoever is free; nobody knows who can cover which task; one absence stops a process.
A list of qualifications exists but is out of date; training is planned when someone leaves; single points of knowledge are known but not fixed.
A current skills matrix for the area; a training plan covers the gaps; new starters are trained on the standard and signed off.
Cover per task and shift is measured against a target; cross-training is scheduled; training is checked by observation.
People train each other and own the matrix; cover is at target on every shift; career steps are linked to skills and improvement work.
dimensions.advice: Build the skills matrix of the area with the team leads and mark every task that only one person per shift can do. Plan cross-training for those first, trained on the standard and signed off.
dimensions.action: Skills matrix for {area} and a cross-training plan for single-person tasks
dimensions.check: Every key task covered by at least two trained people per shift

dimensions.name: Continuous improvement (kaizen)
statements: There is a simple way to raise an idea (board, card or app), and every idea gets an answer within two weeks.
The team carries out small improvements itself every week, without waiting for a project.
Bigger improvements run as kaizen events or projects with a goal in numbers and a check after 30 days.
The results of improvements (time, errors, cost, safety) are measured and shown, and the gain is kept in the standard.
levels: Improvement is a one-off project from management or a consultant; ideas from the floor get lost; changes fade within weeks.
An idea board or box exists, but few ideas are carried out and answers are slow; improvement depends on a few enthusiasts.
The idea board is reviewed every week; most ideas get an answer and an owner; a few kaizen events a year with measured results.
Ideas raised and carried out are tracked; kaizen events follow a standard with a 30-day check; results are kept in the standard.
Improvement is part of everyone's job: many small ideas per person and year, events chosen from the value stream, results shared across sites.
dimensions.advice: Put up a kaizen board in the area and review it at the same time every week: every idea gets an answer and an owner within two weeks. Run one kaizen event a quarter on the biggest gap.
dimensions.action: Start a weekly kaizen board review in {area}
dimensions.check: Every idea answered within two weeks; ideas carried out per month

tips: Score what you see, not what is planned.
A standard in a binder that nobody follows is level 2, not 3. Walk the floor while you score.
Each assessor scores alone first. Where two scores lie two levels or more apart, the tool flags it: discuss what each one saw before you agree.
N/A only when it truly does not apply.
A statement that does not fit the area is left out of the average. A gap is not N/A: score it 1.
Same area, same statements, ideally the same assessors. The radar shows the change against the last assessment.
Take the three weakest dimensions to the Action Tracker, each with an owner and a check, and leave the rest for the next quarter.
